distractorNotes.C: The AV valves are OPEN during atrial systole, allowing the atrial kick to push blood into the ventricles -- the opposite of closed.

which-of-the-following-is-associated-wit.explanation: Venous obstruction impedes the return of blood to the heart, reducing ventricular preload (end-diastolic filling) -- and per the Frank-Starling mechanism, reduced preload directly decreases stroke volume and therefore cardiac output. This is the opposite effect from increased blood volume, increased end-diastolic volume, or increased myocardial contractility, all of which enhance either preload or the heart's pumping efficiency and therefore tend to INCREASE, not decrease, cardiac output.

distractorNotes.A: Increased blood volume typically raises venous return and preload, tending to increase (not decrease) cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
distractorNotes.B: Increased end-diastolic volume (preload) directly increases stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism, increasing (not decreasing) cardiac output.
distractorNotes.D: Increased myocardial contractility directly increases stroke volume and cardiac output, the opposite of a decrease.

which-of-the-following-is-the-normal-ord.explanation: The correct sequential order of the cardiac cycle's diastolic-to-systolic transition is: rapid filling phase, followed by the reduced filling phase (diastasis), followed by atrial systole, followed by isovolumetric contraction as ventricular systole begins -- exactly the order given in this option. This sequence correctly reflects the physiology: after the initial burst of passive rapid filling and the slower diastasis phase, the atria contract to top off ventricular filling just before the ventricles begin their own isovolumetric contraction, building pressure with all valves closed before ejection can begin.

distractorNotes.A: This sequence incorrectly places reduced ejection (a systolic phase) before atrial systole, and isovolumetric relaxation (which should precede rapid filling) after atrial systole, scrambling the correct order.
distractorNotes.C: This sequence incorrectly places isovolumetric relaxation after rapid filling (it should precede it) and puts rapid ejection and atrial systole in the wrong relative order.
distractorNotes.D: This sequence incorrectly places reduced ejection before rapid ejection (rapid ejection should come first) and puts isovolumetric contraction after both ejection phases instead of before them.

about-the-cardiac-muscle-all-the-followi.explanation: Cardiac muscle forms a FUNCTIONAL syncytium, not a true (anatomical) syncytium: individual cardiac muscle cells remain structurally distinct, each with its own nucleus and cell membrane, but are electrically coupled via low-resistance gap junctions at the intercalated discs, allowing action potentials to spread rapidly between cells so the tissue behaves AS IF it were a single continuous unit. This is a critical distinction from a true syncytium (a single continuous mass of cytoplasm shared among many nuclei, as seen in skeletal muscle fibres or the placental syncytiotrophoblast), making the claim that cardiac muscle forms a 'true' syncytium the false statement here. The other statements are correct: intercalated discs do have low electrical resistance (via gap junctions), cardiac muscle does obey the all-or-none law (each chamber contracts maximally or not at all, owing to its functional syncytial spread of excitation), and cardiac muscle is exceptionally richly supplied with capillaries, with roughly one capillary per muscle fibre.

distractorNotes.A: True: the intercalated discs' gap junctions provide low electrical resistance, enabling rapid, coordinated spread of excitation between cardiac muscle cells.
distractorNotes.C: True: because excitation spreads through the functional syncytium to the whole chamber, cardiac muscle obeys the all-or-none law at the level of each chamber.
distractorNotes.D: True: cardiac muscle's high, continuous metabolic (oxidative) demand is matched by an unusually dense capillary network, approaching one capillary per muscle fibre.

an-effect-of-myocardial-ischemia-on-the-.explanation: Myocardial ischemia depletes the ATP supply needed to power the energy-dependent Na+-K+ ATPase pump, inhibiting its function and disrupting the normal transmembrane ionic gradients -- intracellular Na+ accumulates while K+ leaks out of the ischemic cells into the extracellular space, altering resting and action potentials in a way that predisposes to arrhythmias. This mechanism directly explains why the extracellular environment around ischemic myocardium actually shows local HYPERkalaemia (not hypokalaemia), and why phase 0 of the action potential becomes DEPRESSED (slower rate of rise), not accelerated, as ATP and normal ionic gradients are compromised.

distractorNotes.A: Myocardial ischemia causes local HYPERkalaemia in the extracellular fluid (from impaired Na+-K+ pump function and K+ leaking out of cells), not hypokalaemia.
distractorNotes.C: Ischemia causes ATP DEPLETION within cardiomyocytes (due to inadequate oxygen supply for aerobic metabolism), not ATP accumulation.
distractorNotes.D: Ischemia typically DECREASES, not increases, the slope of phase 0 depolarization, as the compromised metabolic and ionic environment impairs fast sodium channel function.

as-regard-the-standard-limb-leads-of-ecg.explanation: By Einthoven's triangle convention, standard limb Lead II specifically records the potential difference between the left leg and the right arm, forming one side of the triangle formed by the three limb electrode positions. This is distinct from Lead I (left arm minus right arm) and Lead III (left leg minus left arm), and Lead II's orientation, roughly parallel to the heart's mean electrical axis, is why it typically shows the clearest, most representative P-QRS-T waveform and is the lead most commonly used for basic rhythm monitoring.

concerning-the-ecg-of-an-aciult-human-al.explanation: The Q wave is part of the QRS complex and reflects early ventricular (specifically septal) depolarization, not atrial depolarization -- atrial depolarization is represented exclusively by the P wave, which precedes the QRS complex entirely. This makes the claim that the Q wave coincides with atrial depolarization a clear, confidently identifiable error. The other statements are correctly true: the P wave does represent atrial depolarization, a PR interval of 0.3 seconds is indeed prolonged beyond the normal 0.12-0.20 second range and indicates impaired (delayed) AV conduction, and the R wave is commonly associated with the depolarization wavefront reaching the ventricular apex region early in the QRS sequence via the rapidly-conducting Purkinje fibres there.

in-an-ecg-recording-the-time-between-atr.explanation: The P-R segment is the isoelectric portion of the ECG tracing specifically spanning the gap between the end of atrial depolarization (end of the P wave) and the start of ventricular depolarization (beginning of the QRS complex) -- this flat segment represents the physiological delay imposed by slow conduction through the AV node, allowing the atria to finish contracting before the ventricles are activated. This is distinct from the P-R INTERVAL, which additionally includes the P wave itself (measuring from the start of atrial depolarization rather than its end).

distractorNotes.B: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization itself, not the preceding gap between atrial and ventricular depolarization.
